Get started with cohortflow

Source: vignettes/cohortflow.Rmd
cohortflow.Rmd

Most cohort studies and trials report how a starting population was whittled down to the analysed cohort: who was assessed, who was excluded and why, and how many were left at each stage. That record usually ends up scattered across filter() calls, hand-counted tables and a flow diagram drawn in PowerPoint, and the three drift apart as the analysis changes.

cohortflow keeps a single record. You write the eligibility criteria once as a pipeline, apply it to your data, and derive the final cohort, the excluded rows, the attrition table and the CONSORT diagram from the same object, so they always agree.

library(cohortflow)

Example data

The package ships with generators for four common trial designs. Here we use a two-arm parallel-group randomised trial with 300 people assessed for eligibility. Like real data, it is untidy: some ages are missing, some people failed screening or never consented, and some withdrew.

dat <- mock_parallel_rct(n_participants = 300, seed = 2024)
dat
#> # A tibble: 300 × 10
#>    participant_id arm            age age_group sex   ethnicity eligible_screen
#>    <chr>          <chr>        <dbl> <chr>     <chr> <chr>     <lgl>          
#>  1 P0001          Intervention    28 18-39     M     European  TRUE           
#>  2 P0002          Control         44 40-64     F     Pacific   TRUE           
#>  3 P0003          Control         81 65+       M     European  TRUE           
#>  4 P0004          Intervention    64 40-64     M     European  TRUE           
#>  5 P0005          Control         NA NA        M     Pacific   TRUE           
#>  6 P0006          Control          5 <18       F     Maori     TRUE           
#>  7 P0007          Control         50 40-64     M     European  FALSE          
#>  8 P0008          Intervention    40 40-64     F     European  TRUE           
#>  9 P0009          Control         34 18-39     M     Pacific   TRUE           
#> 10 P0010          Intervention    49 40-64     M     European  TRUE           
#> # ℹ 290 more rows
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: consent_date <date>, baseline_complete <lgl>,
#> #   withdrew <lgl>

1. Define the criteria

A pipeline starts with cf_criteria(), and each step is added with a pipe. include() keeps the rows where its condition is TRUE; exclude() drops the rows where its condition is TRUE. Each step has a label for reporting, and steps can share a category so they are reported together.

randomise() removes nobody. It marks the point at which people were allocated, so later reports can show what happened in each arm afterwards.

crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded", reason = "Age missing", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over", reason = "Under 18", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening", reason = "Failed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent") |>
  randomise(by = "participant_id", arms = "arm") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent") |>
  include(~ baseline_complete, label = "Baseline complete", reason = "Baseline incomplete")

crit
#> Cohort criteria pipeline  (7 steps)
#>    1. [+][~] (include) {Age} Age recorded
#>           !is.na(age)
#>           removes: Age missing
#>    2. [+][~] (include) {Age} Aged 18 or over
#>           age >= 18
#>           removes: Under 18
#>    3. [+][~] (include) Passed screening
#>           eligible_screen
#>           removes: Failed screening
#>    4. [+][~] (include) Consented
#>           !is.na(consent_date)
#>           removes: Did not consent
#>    5. [R][-] (randomise) [by: participant_id] [arms: arm] Randomised
#>           <none>
#>    6. [-][~] (exclude) Withdrew consent
#>           withdrew
#>    7. [+][~] (include) Baseline complete
#>           baseline_complete
#>           removes: Baseline incomplete

In the printout, [+] marks an inclusion step, [-] an exclusion and [R] the randomisation point. [~] means the condition is a formula. The Writing criteria article covers every step type.

2. Apply them

apply_criteria() runs the steps in order. Each step sees only the rows that survived the steps before it. id names the column that identifies a row.

flow <- apply_criteria(dat, crit, id = "participant_id")
flow
#> Cohort flow  (7 steps | 300 -> 195 rows | 105 excluded)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
#>    1. [+] Age recorded {Age}
#>        n_in: 300  kept: 285  removed: 15
#>    2. [+] Aged 18 or over {Age}
#>        n_in: 285  kept: 279  removed: 6
#>    3. [+] Passed screening
#>        n_in: 279  kept: 253  removed: 26
#>    4. [+] Consented
#>        n_in: 253  kept: 226  removed: 27
#>    5. [R] Randomised by participant_id arms arm
#>        n_in: 226  kept: 226  removed: 0
#>    6. [-] Withdrew consent
#>        n_in: 226  kept: 218  removed: 8
#>    7. [+] Baseline complete
#>        n_in: 218  kept: 195  removed: 23

The result is a cf_flow: the original data plus a record of which rows each step removed. Everything below is read from it.

3. Get the cohort

cohort() returns the rows that passed every step, and excluded() returns the rows that were removed, labelled with the step that removed them:

final <- cohort(flow)
nrow(final)
#> [1] 195

removed <- excluded(flow)
table(removed$cf_label)
#> 
#>      Age recorded   Aged 18 or over Baseline complete         Consented 
#>                15                 6                23                27 
#>  Passed screening  Withdrew consent 
#>                26                 8

Both take a step selector (a step number, a label or a category), so you can also get the cohort as it stood at an earlier point. For example, here is everyone who was randomised:

nrow(cohort(flow, at = "Consented"))
#> [1] 226

4. Attrition table

as_attrition_tibble() returns the counts as a plain data frame, ready for your own formatting or further calculation:

as_attrition_tibble(flow)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 9
#>    row_type label    indent_level     n n_removed pct_removed post_randomisation
#>    <chr>    <chr>           <int> <int>     <int>       <dbl> <lgl>             
#>  1 header   Assesse…            0   300        NA        NA   FALSE             
#>  2 category Age                 1   300        21         7   FALSE             
#>  3 step     Age rec…            2   300        15         5   FALSE             
#>  4 step     Aged 18…            2   285         6         2   FALSE             
#>  5 step     Passed …            1   279        26         9.3 FALSE             
#>  6 step     Consent…            1   253        27        10.7 FALSE             
#>  7 step     Randomi…            1   226         0         0   TRUE              
#>  8 step     Withdre…            1   226         8         3.5 TRUE              
#>  9 step     Baselin…            1   218        23        10.6 TRUE              
#> 10 final    Final c…            0   195        NA        65   TRUE              
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: Control <int>, Intervention <int>

as_attrition_table() formats the same data with flextable (the default, best for Word), gt or huxtable. Steps that share a category are grouped under one heading, and because there is a randomise() step, the final row is broken out by arm.

as_attrition_table(flow, backend = "gt")
Criterion N Removed % removed Control Intervention
Assessed for eligibility 300



Age 300 21 7.0%

Age recorded 300 15 5.0%

Aged 18 or over 285 6 2.0%

Passed screening 279 26 9.3%

Consented 253 27 10.7%

Randomised 226 — —

Withdrew consent 226 8 3.5%

Baseline complete 218 23 10.6%

Final cohort 195
65.0% included 107 88

The Attrition tables article covers grouped tables, shading and the other backends.

5. CONSORT flow diagram

as_consort_diagram() draws the flow. Up to the randomisation box there is one shared trunk. After it, each arm gets its own column, so post-allocation losses are reported separately for each arm, as CONSORT asks.

diagram <- as_consort_diagram(flow)
diagram

Each main box shows how many people remain after a step, and each side box how many that step removed, each beside text that describes those people. An inclusion step’s label (“Passed screening”) goes on the main box and its reason (“Failed screening”) on the side box. An exclusion step’s label (“Withdrew consent”) goes on the side box, and the main box below it reads “Remaining”. A category’s side box lists the reason for each of its steps (here, Age).

The diagram is a ggplot. Save it for a manuscript with save_consort_diagram(), which picks the format from the file extension and sizes the page so the text fits its boxes:

save_consort_diagram(diagram, "consort.pdf")
save_consort_diagram(diagram, "consort.png", dpi = 300)

The CONSORT diagrams article covers styling and other trial designs.

6. Who was excluded?

Reviewers often ask whether exclusions changed the make-up of the cohort. as_characteristics_table() summarises chosen variables at every step, in one column per step:

as_characteristics_table(
  flow,
  vars = c("age", "sex"),
  steps = list(0, "Consented", "Baseline complete"),
  var_labels = c(age = "Age, years", sex = "Sex"),
  backend = "gt"
)
Characteristic Assessed for eligibility (n = 300) Consented (n = 226) Baseline complete (n = 195)
Age, years
Mean (SD) 46.8 (14.5) 47.7 (13.7) 47.4 (13.2)
Missing 15 (5.0%) 0 (0.0%) 0 (0.0%)
Sex
F 146 (48.7%) 114 (50.4%) 103 (52.8%)
M 144 (48.0%) 106 (46.9%) 86 (44.1%)
O 10 (3.3%) 6 (2.7%) 6 (3.1%)

Use excluded = TRUE to describe the people removed at each step instead. The Describing who was excluded article covers this and overlapping exclusion reasons.

Missing values. A condition that gives NA is treated differently by the two step types. include(~ age >= 18) removes a row with a missing age; exclude(~ age < 18) keeps it. Here 15 people have no recorded age, so the choice changes the denominator. This pipeline makes the choice visible with a separate “Age recorded” step. See Missing values for a worked example.

7. Writing it up

The methods section usually describes the same flow in words. as_narrative() writes that paragraph from the flow, so its numbers match the table and the diagram. Each step is described by its reason, and after randomisation each sentence gives the counts for each arm:

as_narrative(flow)

Of 300 participants assessed for eligibility, 21 (7.0%) were excluded: age missing (n = 15) and under 18 (n = 6). A further 26 (9.3%) were excluded (failed screening). A further 27 (10.7%) were excluded (did not consent), leaving 226. The remaining 226 were randomised to Control (n = 121) and Intervention (n = 105). After randomisation, 3 (2.5%) in Control and 5 (4.8%) in Intervention were excluded (withdrew consent). A further 11 (9.3%) in Control and 12 (12.0%) in Intervention were excluded (baseline incomplete). The final cohort comprised 195 participants (65.0% of those assessed): 107 in Control and 88 in Intervention.

Use style = "bullets" to get one sentence per line, which is easier to edit into a draft. Set unit to the noun your study counts (for example “patients”). Read the text through and adapt it to the journal’s style.

as_narrative(flow, style = "bullets", unit = "people")
  • Of 300 people assessed for eligibility, 21 (7.0%) were excluded: age missing (n = 15) and under 18 (n = 6).
  • A further 26 (9.3%) were excluded (failed screening).
  • A further 27 (10.7%) were excluded (did not consent), leaving 226.
  • The remaining 226 were randomised to Control (n = 121) and Intervention (n = 105).
  • After randomisation, 3 (2.5%) in Control and 5 (4.8%) in Intervention were excluded (withdrew consent).
  • A further 11 (9.3%) in Control and 12 (12.0%) in Intervention were excluded (baseline incomplete).
  • The final cohort comprised 195 people (65.0% of those assessed): 107 in Control and 88 in Intervention.

8. Save the criteria

A criteria pipeline can be written to YAML and read back, so the exact definitions can be kept under version control, shared with collaborators or attached to a protocol:

yml <- export_criteria(crit)
cat(yml)
#> cohortflow_criteria:
#>   version: 1
#>   steps:
#>   - label: Age recorded
#>     type: include
#>     kind: formula
#>     by: ~
#>     expr: '!is.na(age)'
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: Age
#>     arms: ~
#>     reason: Age missing
#>   - label: Aged 18 or over
#>     type: include
#>     kind: formula
#>     by: ~
#>     expr: age >= 18
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: Age
#>     arms: ~
#>     reason: Under 18
#>   - label: Passed screening
#>     type: include
#>     kind: formula
#>     by: ~
#>     expr: eligible_screen
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: ~
#>     arms: ~
#>     reason: Failed screening
#>   - label: Consented
#>     type: include
#>     kind: formula
#>     by: ~
#>     expr: '!is.na(consent_date)'
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: ~
#>     arms: ~
#>     reason: Did not consent
#>   - label: Randomised
#>     type: randomise
#>     kind: none
#>     by: participant_id
#>     expr: ~
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: ~
#>     arms: arm
#>   - label: Withdrew consent
#>     type: exclude
#>     kind: formula
#>     by: ~
#>     expr: withdrew
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: ~
#>     arms: ~
#>   - label: Baseline complete
#>     type: include
#>     kind: formula
#>     by: ~
#>     expr: baseline_complete
#>     fn_ref: ~
#>     category: ~
#>     arms: ~
#>     reason: Baseline incomplete

identical(
  as_attrition_tibble(apply_criteria(dat, import_criteria(text = yml), id = "participant_id")),
  as_attrition_tibble(flow)
)
#> [1] TRUE

Pass path = to export_criteria() and import_criteria() to write and read a file instead.
